ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: The p‑value quantifies how likely an observed result could arise if the null hypothesis were true. In research it guides whether findings are considered statistically significant.

sections.p: A p‑value is the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as observed, assuming no real effect (null hypothesis). It is calculated from a test statistic.
Statistical significance does not measure effect size or clinical importance; consider confidence intervals and real‑world impact alongside the p‑value.
A low p‑value can result from a true effect, large sample size, or data bias. A high p‑value may stem from no effect, small sample, or high variability.
In study reports, p‑values appear next to test statistics (e.g., χ² = 10.5, p = 0.001) indicating the strength of evidence against H₀.
Choosing the correct statistical test depends on data type, distribution, and study design.

sections.p: Relying solely on p‑values can mislead: statistically significant results may be clinically trivial, and non‑significant results may hide important effects.
Interpret p‑values within the broader evidence hierarchy: assess study quality, effect size, confidence intervals, and plausibility before changing practice.
When planning new research, pre‑specify hypotheses, sample size, and analysis plan to avoid post‑hoc fishing that inflates false‑positive rates.
P‑value is not the same as the probability that H₀ is true, nor is it the same as the effect size or clinical relevance.
Small p‑values from huge datasets may reflect trivial differences; large p‑values from under‑powered studies may miss real effects.
